newsitem.title: INDIA: India watches Chinese defence spending.
newsitem.headline: India watches Chinese defence spending.

text.p: India said on Monday it was cautiously studying China's proposed 14.7 percent increase in defence spending over the previous year, but analysts gave a mixed response to the $9.7 billion allocated for 1997.
"We always take a cautious view of Chinese military spending," a foreign ministry official told Reuters. "We are studying the implications of the latest increase."
China said on Sunday it envisages spending 80.57 billion yuan ($9.7 billion) on defence in 1997, an increase of 14.7 percent over last year's budget.

"The latest budget increase underlines China's steady modernisation in the conventional and non-conventional military areas since the end of Cold War," defence analyst Brahma Chellaney of the Centre for Policy Rersearch told Reuters.
"It comes at a time when China is asserting its national interest in the region, for instance over Taiwan," he said. "This has implications for India as well."
Other analysts said the Chinese economy was dogged by inflation among other problems which would prevent Beijing from taking any bold moves in military spending.
"In real terms it may not be a very significant increase," said Sridhar (one name) of Delhi's state-funded Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses.
"In the contex of India, China is not reported to have made any significant strides in high altitude warfare," Sridhar said.
India and China fought a brief war over their Himalayan borders in 1962, but they signed a peace treaty in 1993.
Some military experts say China's actual defence spending was twice the budgeted amount, with budgets hidden or passed off as science and technology and other expenditure.
China's defence budget was announced two days after India increased its own military spending by a rare 23 percent.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram allocated 356.20 billion rupees ($9.9 billion) in the annual budget for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March) against 294.98 billion the previous year.
Chidambaram also promised to provide additional funds for the military's capital expenditure, if needed, later this year.

Analysts have said New Delhi might be tempted to consider going nuclear to beef up its defences in the short term to stem the erosion in the defence budget, estimated last year to be 2.26 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
